ogTitle: Fetu Afahye: Cape Coast in September
subtitle: Cape Coast’s week of cleansing and thanksgiving
answer: Fetu Afahye is the festival of the chiefs and people of Oguaa, Cape Coast, in the Central Region. It is held over the first week of September and peaks on the first Saturday with a carnival-like procession of chiefs under state umbrellas and the town’s seven Asafo companies. It began as a cleansing after a plague and remains a thanksgiving that brings families home.

sticky.title: First Saturday of September
sticky.text: Find a spot on the procession route through the old town early.

sections.title: Where Fetu Afahye comes from
sections.html:
Tradition tells of a plague that struck Cape Coast; the people prayed to their gods for deliverance and began the festival in thanksgiving and as protection against another outbreak. The name is often traced to efin tu, “doing away with dirt”.[[3]]

During the colonial period the festival was banned for a time, and it was nicknamed “Black Christmas”.[[3]] Today it is a week to remember the ancestors and to bring families home from across Ghana and abroad.[[1]]

days.label: Late August
days.title: The Fosu lagoon opens
days.html: After a month-long ban, chiefs and people lift the ban on fishing in the Fosu lagoon with rites. In 2022 three of the seven Asafo companies, Bentsir, Nkum and Anaafo, held a canoe regatta, and the Omanhen’s net was cast three times to foretell the year’s harvest.[[1]]

days.label: The week
days.title: Purification
days.html: Chiefs, queen mothers and priests process through the town, stopping at shrines for purification rites.[[1]]

days.label: First Saturday
days.title: The grand procession
days.html: The climax: chiefs in palanquins under state umbrellas, Asafo companies with their flags, drumming, dancing and musket fire through the streets of Cape Coast.[[2,3]]

sections.title: Good to know if you go
tips: Where: the procession winds through the old town near Cape Coast Castle.
Book early: Cape Coast fills up for the festival weekend.
Musketry: guns are fired during the procession. Keep a distance and protect children’s ears.
Respect the rites: some rituals are sacred and not for cameras. Ask before photographing chiefs, priests or anyone taking part, and follow what the ushers ask.
While you’re there: Cape Coast Castle, Kakum National Park and Elmina are close. See the Central region page.

faq.a: Over the first week of September each year, with the grand procession on the first Saturday.
It began as a cleansing and thanksgiving after a plague in Cape Coast, and today remembers the ancestors and brings families home.

faq.q: How many Asafo companies does Cape Coast have?
faq.a: Seven, including Bentsir, Nkum and Anaafo.
